transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, Doctor, I’m here because... well, for months now, the property manager and certain people in my building have been trying to pressure me out of my apartment. It’s a very coordinated effort. They’ve been using misdelivered mail, timed noises in the walls... which, speaking of the walls, they did a terrible job with the insulation when they renovated a few years back. The contractor they hired, this fellow with a loud green truck who always parked across two

Aside from these concerns about your neighbors, have you noticed any recent periods where your mood, energy, or sleep needs have changed dramatically—like feeling unusually high, energetic, or needing very little sleep, or conversely feeling very low and hopeless?

No, no, my mood is perfectly fine. I'm not depressed or... or bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I sleep a solid seven or eight hours, actually. I think it helps that I invested in a very good mattress a few years back. It’s one of those firm memory foam ones, you know? I bought it over at the Sears before they closed the location out by the interstate. 

It’s a real shame what happened to Sears, honestly. In my line of work—I’m a management analyst—I actually looked into their corporate restructuring back in the late nineties. If they had just leveraged their real estate assets differently when the big box stores started taking over... I mean, they had all that prime anchor-store square footage and they just sat on it. Typical top-heavy corporate paralysis, nobody wanted to adapt to the supply chain shifts. 

But, um... what were you asking? Oh, right, my energy levels. No, no, my energy is completely normal. It's really just the stress of the property manager constantly trying to... well, you know.
Have you ever heard voices, sounds, or other things that other people around you couldn't hear or perceive?

No, no voices. I don't hear anything like that. I mean, I hear the noises in the walls, but that's just them, you know, banging around. It's not like I'm hearing things that aren't there. My hearing is actually quite good for my age. I had it checked last year when I renewed my driver's license. The DMV over on 4th Street, they have a new system now. It used to take all day, but now you can make an appointment online. 

Although, the website they use is terribly designed. From an analytical standpoint, the user interface is just a disaster. I actually drafted a memo about it, just for my own amusement, outlining how they could streamline the data entry process. If they just integrated the vision and hearing test results directly into the main database instead of having the clerk input it manually... it's a huge bottleneck. It's exactly the kind of inefficiency I used to consult on back when I was working with the state agencies. We saved the Department of Transportation nearly two million dollars in the first quarter alone just by reorganizing their procurement workflow. 

But no, to answer your question, no voices. Just the regular noises, and of course, the things the property manager does.
How long have you been noticing and thinking about these efforts by the property manager and others to push you out of your apartment—weeks, months, or longer?

Well, let's see... it started shortly after I moved in, so it's been about 11 months now. I moved in right around the time the leaves were starting to turn. I always loved autumn in this city. The oak trees down by the park, they get this brilliant rusty orange color. I used to take a walk through that park every Sunday morning before they put in that new coffee shop on the corner. 

Not that I have anything against coffee shops, mind you, but the foot traffic it brought completely changed the character of the neighborhood. And the prices! Seven dollars for a latte? It's absurd. From an economic standpoint, the markup on espresso beverages is staggering. When I analyzed the retail food sector back in 2015, we found that the profit margins on specialty drinks were driving the entire expansion strategy for those franchise models. They essentially sell milk and water at a premium by branding the experience. It's brilliant marketing, really, but terrible for the consumer. 

Anyway, yes, about 11 months of this coordinated effort since I got the new place.
Aside from your concerns about the property manager, has this situation affected your ability to work, socialize, or manage your daily responsibilities over these past 11 months?

Well, it has, unfortunately. I’ve actually had to pull back from several of my consulting contracts lately. Instead of settling into my normal work routine—or even my painting, I used to do watercolors on the weekends—I spend most of my week following up with neighbors, making calls to the corporate office, and trying to get answers from the building staff. 

Speaking of watercolors, I had this lovely set of Windsor & Newton paints I bought during a trip to London back in '08. The pigment quality is just exceptional compared to the student-grade stuff you find here. I used to paint landscapes mostly. There’s a specific technique for doing skies, you know, a wet-on-wet wash that lets the colors bleed naturally to create cloud formations. It requires a very specific type of paper, ideally a 140-pound cold-pressed cotton. If you use the cheap wood-pulp paper, it just buckles and ruins the whole effect. 

I actually did a cost-benefit analysis once for an art supply distributor, looking at their inventory turnover rates for professional versus amateur materials. It turns out the profit is all in the mid-tier products, the ones marketed to hobbyists who think they’re buying professional quality. The margins on those are incredible. 

But yes, I just don't have the time for painting or my regular work right now. Not with everything I have to keep track of around the building.

Aside from the situation with your property manager and neighbors, have you noticed any other unusual experiences or beliefs—things that seem important or connected to you in a special way that others might not see the same way?

No, nothing else like that. I mean, the issue with the property manager is more than enough to deal with, isn't it? I don't need anything else going on. Although, speaking of things people don't see the same way... I was reading the other day about how color perception actually degrades as we age, specifically in the blue-yellow spectrum. The lens of the eye slowly yellows over time, which acts like a filter. 

It makes me wonder about the lighting they installed in the hallways last month. They switched everything to these cheap LED fixtures. From a procurement standpoint, I understand the appeal—the energy savings over a five-year lifecycle are substantial, and the maintenance costs drop significantly because the bulbs last so much longer. But the color temperature is completely wrong for a residential corridor. It's a harsh 5000-Kelvin daylight bulb, which is terrible for the circadian rhythm if you're out there in the evening. When I consulted for the hospital administration board back in 2012, we did a massive overhaul of the lighting in the patient wards. We found that switching to warmer, dimmable lights in the evening actually reduced patient agitation and sleep disturbances by nearly 18 percent. The data was absolutely conclusive. 

But no, to your point, I don't have any other unusual beliefs or anything like that. Just the very real situation with the building management.

opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre persecutory delusion (organized effort by property manager/neighbors to force him out) persisting for approximately 11 months, without hallucinations, disorganized speech (aside from tangential/circumstantial style consistent with personality, not thought disorder), negative symptoms, or mood episode features (denies mania/depression, sleep and energy normal). The delusion is encapsulated with resulting functional impairment (withdrawal from consulting work and hobbies) but overall functioning outside the delusional theme remains relatively preserved. This profile—single, well-systematized non-bizarre delusion >1 month, absence of hallucinations/other psychotic symptoms, and no mood disorder—meets criteria for Delusional Disorder (F22) rather than Schizophrenia (which requires additional first-rank symptoms or more pervasive impairment) or a mood disorder with psychotic features (denied mood symptoms).
